1	=================== PDF 404
2	SUPERTRAINING
3	STRENGTH TRAINING 
4	METHODS
5	The preceding chapters have extracted many of the principles, means and methods of strength training, but it 
6	cannot be claimed that the task of presenting an exhaustive holistic system is complete. Many further steps have 
7	to be taken to produce an integrated system of strength conditioning, guided by thorough research and examination 
8	of practical methods implemented by anyone for whom the quest for strength is important. As mentioned in 
9	Chapter 1, the sources of information on the art and science of strength training are the following:
10	• Weighdifting and Powerlifting
11	• Bodybuilding
12	• Supplementary resistance training
13	• Physical therapy
14	• Scientific research
15	The weight training gymnasium, whose origins lie in Grecian and pre-Grecian times, has provided a natural 
16	laboratory replete with subjects who have used weightlifting, powerlifting or bodybuilding to explore the 
17	boundaries of human muscle development for their specific purposes. It should not be surprising that this should 
18	have becomc a fertile setting for experientially discovering strength training methods. Weightlifters have become 
19	experts at developing explosive strength and skill, bodybuilders at producing massive hypertrophy and low body 
20	(at, and powerliftcrs at developing slow speed and maximal isometric strength.
21	Only in recent years, has science begun to investigate seriously the foundations, validity and scope of the 
22	vast amount of practical information gathered by several generations of adherents of the 'Iron Game'. 
23	Consequently, resistance training is rapidly losing stigmas such as 'slowing one down', 'making one muscle-bound', 
24	decreasing flexibility’ and 'causing back injury'. 
25	Scientists entering the field of strength training have been 
26	surprised at the enormous body of knowledge accumulated by competitors in the strength sports and have been 
27	devoting their ingenuity to devise reproducible experiments to investigate all training methods for different 
28	subjects at different stages of fitness. Their research has also led them to add to this encyclopaedia of strength 
29	training techniques various methods taken from other sports requiring the display of different types of strength 
30	fitness, in particular, track-and-field. Thus, plyometrics, circuit training and cross training became recognised as 
31	valuable training methods.
32	Few coaches have realised that physiotherapy also offers many useful adjunct methods of musculoskeletal 
33	and neuromuscular training, such as electrostimuiation, accelerated recuperation and PNF (proprioceptive 
34	neuromuscular facilitation). Because of the broad scope of training offered by PNF, this system is discussed in 
35	detail later in this chapter.
36	As has been stressed throughout this text, all strength training depends on two dominant factors (e.g. see Ch 
37	I), namely structural conditioning and functional (central nervous and neuromuscular) conditioning. 
38	Thus, 
39	strength training may be categorised according to its 
40	major structural and functional aims relative to the 
41	importance of nervous system training methods (Fig 7.1). The numerous methods and techniques of training may 
42	then be added hierarchically below each of these major aims.
43	It is tempting to attempt to devise a single extensive flowchart to categorise and interrelate all of the better 
44	known methods of resistance training, but the extent of overlap between the different methods makes the final 
45	result logically tedious, unattractive and largely unusable. Instead, it is simpler to organise the different methods 
46	as a loosely interconnected array of columns and rows, showing only some of the more obvious relationships (Fig 
47	7.2). The merit of this type of chart is that it enables one to see at a glance the variety o f many of the methods 
48	which were discussed in previous chapters. Where necessary, any terminology and methods that did not appear 
49	explicitly in the book are described later, so as to furnish the reader with a compendium of methods for practical 
50	application.
51	In using the summary depicted in Figure 7.2, it is important to note that some of the training methods may be 
52	used to achieve several different aims by altering variables such as the load, number of repetitions and rest 
53	intervals. For example, pyramiding should not be regarded merely as a bodybuilding method, because it may also
54	7 S '
55	393
56	
57	=================== PDF 405
58	SUPERTRAININC,
59	be used in the earlier preparatory stages to meet several general training aims such as increased muscic 
60	hypertrophy, strength and endurance, depending on the load and number o f repetitions (which are inversely 
61	related). Therefore, pyramiding has been classified separately to show the different forms of pyramiding that arc 
62	commonly used in the broad field of strength training.
63	Figure 7.1 Broad classification o f the major aims o f strength training. The development of power refers to the qualities of strength- 
64	speed and speed-strength, as discussed throughout this text.
65	The method of quasi-isometrics occurs as a natural consequence of training with near-maximal loads, since it is 
66	impossible to move any heavy load at high speed without the use of ballistic techniques. However, there is a 
67	discrete method of quasi-isometrics (nowadays popularised in bodybuilding circles as the superslow method), 
68	which entails performing very slow controlled repetitions with even moderately heavy or lighter loads. In this 
69	case the athlete chooses to move the load slowly; with heavier weights he has no option but to move slowly.
70	Flexibility training has not been elaborated upon beyond its broad subdivision into static, active and other 
71	forms, since details o f its development were discussed earlier in depth (3.5). It should also be noted that several 
72	of the other training methods with heavy resistance used over a full range of movement constitute very effective 
73	means of active stretching.
74	In organising any training programme, it should always be remembered that great emphasis should be placed 
75	on increasing the mass and strength of the connective tissues, such as the tendons, ligaments, cartilages and joint 
76	capsules, particularly during the early stages of training and transition phases to levels of higher competitive 
77	intensity (see 1.6.2). An essential part o f the general preparatory phase of all training is also low intensity, 
78	prolonged cyclical activity to enhance cardiovascular and circulatory processes, as well as capillarisation in all the 
79	relevant muscle groups. This same type of activity can also play a useful role in restoration between intensive 
80	training sessions and phases.
81	7.1 Bodybuilding and O ther Strength Training Methods
82	The selection of any resistance training method to achieve a desired training effect may be determined on the basis 
83	of competitive experience and research into the phenomena of strength, adaptation, specificity and 
84	supercompensation, which were discussed in great detail in the preceding chapters. 
85	The various resistance 
86	training methods are categorised according to the general scheme presented in Figure 7.2.
87	In doing so, it is important to appreciate that certain methods classified under one heading may sometimes 
88	also be used to produce effects falling under other headings. 
89	For instance, cheating and restricted range 
90	repetitions, although classified as supramaximal methods, may also be used submaximally or circamaximally. It 
91	the role of the coach to choose a given method according to the intended training goal and adapt it accordingly. In 
92	this regard. Table 1.1, which was based largely on the practical experience o f generations of bodybuilders and 
93	weightlifters, may serve as an initial guide to be viewed in the light of the scheme depicted in Figure 7.1.
94	The choice between a focus on hypertrophy or nervous system training may be based on performance in tests 
95	of explosive strength and speed-strength (e.g. vertical jump), as well as on the magnitude of the strength deficit 
96	discussed early in Chapter 1. If this deficit at any stage is large, then it would be appropriate to concentrate more 
97	on weightlifting and reactive methods, whereas, if the deficit is small, submaximal bodybuilding methods should be 
98	relied upon.
99	394
100	
101	=================== PDF 406
102	SUPERTRAINING
103	Figure 7.2 Extended categorisation of the different forms of strength training for different structural and functional purposes.
104	Maximal Methods
105	Weightlifting Method This method is characterised by single repetition explosive sets or low repetition sets (2-3 
106	reps), in which each repetition is separated from the next by a short rest period (1-5 minutes, depending on how 
107	close the load is to a I RM). Sometimes this method is referred to as the interval set method. This IRM set with 
108	optimal recovery intervals between sets has been adopted by bodybuilders as the rest-pause method, which also
109	395
110	
111	=================== PDF 407
112	SUPERTRAINING
113	involves doing sets of IRM, but with rest periods of 10-20 seconds. 
114	This shorter rest is possible, sincc 
115	bodybuilding movements do not require the high levels of skill, speed and coordination of the Olympic lifts.
116	Maximal or circa-maximal concentrics This is a variation of the above method in which the concentric phase of a 
117	IRM or near IRM lift is completed, then the bar is allowed to drop to its starting position without being 
118	controlled by the muscles. In its weightlifting form, the athlete loads the bar with rubber bumper plates so that he 
119	can drop it from its final position to the platform so as to avoid executing the depleting eccentric lowering phase. 
120	In bodybuilding, a partner usually assists in the lowering (or eccentric) phase.
121	Maximal isometrics Maximal slow isometrics or explosive isometrics (see 4.2.4) are executed in single or few 
122	repetition sets lasting about 5 seconds with rest intervals of 2-3 minutes between sets.
123	Maximal eccentrics This method (see 4.2.5) involves taking a maximal eccentric weight (about 30-40% greater 
124	than one's maximum concentric lift) from racks or from a starting position in which the load is raised by a partner. 
125	The load is carefully controlled until the end position is reached, when the partner lifts it through the concentric 
126	phase again. Note that, although similar to the 'forced reps' method, the eccentric method (or 'negatives') docs not 
127	require the athlete to produce any concentric contraction. Often the eccentric method is regarded as one of the 
128	'supramaximal' methods and as such, carries an increased risk of injury. Eccentrics are associated with greater 
129	muscle soreness than most other methods and should not be used too frequently. Its dangers can be reduced by 
130	selecting the load carefully and avoiding sudden changes in movement velocity or trajectory.
131	Supramaximal Methods
132	Forced repetitions This method involves working to failure with a given load, then executing a few more 
133	repetitions with the aid of a training partner, who provides the minimal assistance necessary to enable the 
134	concentric phase to be completed successfully. The eccentric phase of the exercise is carried out without help.
135	Restricted range repetitions The athlete chooses a load which is heavier than the maximum that he can use for the 
136	complete cycle of the exercise, then he performs a few small range concentric-eccentric repetitions near his 
137	strongest region of action for that exercise. If these repetitions are performed at the end of a normal 5-8 
138	repetition concentric-eccentric set to the point where the muscles begin to 'bum', this method is known as burning 
139	reps to the body-building fraternity. One may also execute concentric or eccentric restricted range movements 
140	with the aid of a partner (as with the forced repetition method).
141	In weightlifting or powerlifting, an exercise may be performed over a specific range with a load greater than 
142	one's capability for the full movement to rectify any deficit of strength in that region. Typical examples are 
143	pulling exercises around knee-to-lower thigh level and squats or bench presses in the range of one's 'sticking point'. 
144	Power racks or plinths are commonly to secure the weight in a given starting position. Restricted range exercises 
145	may also be done with maximal or submaximal loads, depending on one's training purpose.
146	Cheating This method involves the use of momentum, bouncing of the bar against the body, swaying the body, 
147	using accessory muscles or otherwise completing an exercise by deviating from its traditionally strict form. This 
148	may be done to complete any exercise with weights heavier than one's I RM or at the end of a fairly heavy set 
149	which has taken one to the point of failure. There are recommended safe ways of cheating and these must be 
150	followed religiously if injury is to be avoided.
151	Ballistics This method is sometimes regarded as a form o f cheating and involves lowering or dropping a weight 
152	rapidly to recruit the myotatic stretch reflex or exploit the stored elastic energy in the tendons and other 
153	connective tissues. Although this method is classified as supramaximal, the training load is not necessarily 
154	supramaximal; rather, it is the resulting muscle tension that reaches this level of intensity.
155	Circa-maximal Methods
156	These methods, which may involve all of the preceding methods, implicate training with loads that are close to 
157	one's IRM (characteristically about 90-97.5% of IRM). The main difference between maximal and circa-maximal 
158	methods is that the latter may be performed with several successive repetitions without a prolonged rest interval.
159	Submaximal Methods
160	Submaximal or repetition methods characteristically involve training with loads of about 60-80% of one's IRM to 
161	the point of failure on the last set. 
162	The smaller loads enable the exercise to be performed with multiple 
163	repetitions, mainly for bodybuilding reasons such as hypertrophy or muscle definition.
164	396
165	
166	=================== PDF 408
167	SUPERTRAINING
168	I Classical Bodybuilding Regime This is one of the best known elementary bodybuilding methods and involves 
169	3 to 5 sets of 8-10 repetitions with the same load, allowing a rest interval of 2-5 minutes between sets. This may 
170	also be regarded as a particular case of the plateau system of training with an unchanging load. Another classical 
171	method involves increasing the load with each set so that the athlete is compelled to progressively decrease the 
172	number of repetitions from 10 in the first set to 4-5 repetitions in the last set. The rest interval increases as the 
173	load increases. This is a typical form of the pyramid system of training.
174	B. Extensive Bodybuilding Regime This high volume method involves 3-5 sets of 15-20 repetitions with a load of 
175	about 60-70%. The rest interval between sets is 2-3 minutes, increasing with increase in load from set to set.
176	C Intensive Bodybuilding Regime This high intensity method involves 3-5 sets of 5-8 repetitions with a load of 
177	80-90% (see Figs 1.8 and 1.9). The heavier loads mean that the rest interval between sets should be between 2-5 
178	minutes, increasing with increase in load.
179	Each of the preceding regimes may use the following methods which have been defined earlier: forced repetitions, 
180	cheating, eccentrics (negatives), burning repetitions and ballistics. 
181	In addition, the following methods are 
182	popularly used:
183	Supersets A superset usually consists of two separate exercises in which the athlete performs set 1 of exercise 1, 
184	moves immediately to set 1 of exercise 2, then performs set 2 of exercise 1, set 2 of exercise 2 and so on until the 
185	chosen number of sets is completed. Since supersets are not intended to develop strength, the athlete allows little 
186	or no rest between sets. Sometimes supersets involve more than two exercises, in which case it is probably more 
187	appropriate to refer to the extended method as multi-setting. A well-known type of multi-set is the giant set, 
188	which comprises 4-6 different exercises performed in a mini-circuit.
189	Pre-exhaustion This involves performing a single-joint exercise which preferentially exhausts one of the muscle 
190	groups that will be used in the following multi-joint exercisc. Not only docs this work the one muscle group 
191	intensively, but it compels other muscles to act strongly as accessory muscles. For example, if supine dumbbell 
192	flyes are performed before a bench press, the pectoral and anterior deltoid muscles are pre-exhausted and the 
193	triceps are forced to bccome more vigorously involved.
194	Repetitions to Failure This method simply involves continuing the exercise until it is impossible to execute 
195	another repetition without assistance. It is often used for muscle endurance and definition training.
196	Split Routine This system involves dividing a routine into two distinct components, each of which trains a 
197	different body zone in successive workouts. For example, upper body exercises may be done on one day, 
198	followed by lower body exercises the next day. Another system may involve flexor and adductor training on one 
199	day, with extensor and abductor training on the next day. Sometimes, the advanced athlete may execute one part 
200	of the split early in the day and the other part later. A common weekly split routine prescribes split training on 
201	Monday-Tucsday, resting on Wednesday, more split training on Thursday-Friday, completed by a weekend of 
202	passive or active rest.
203	Plateau Method After a specific warmup with a light weight, the load remains constant for 3-4 sets (e.g. 50 x 10, 
204	70 x 6, 70 x 6, 70 x 6). This method is commonly used during the early stages of training novices or for 
205	transitional active rest phases after weeks of heavy training.
206	Step Method The number of repetitions is kept fixed, while the load is increased after each set until the prescribed 
207	number of repetitions can no longer be maintained (e.g. 60 x 3, 70 x 3, 80 x 3, 85 x 3).
208	Stripping (Descending Set) Method Some bodybuilders also use the name ‘Drop Sets’ for this method. 
209	It 
210	involves working progressively with an increasing load and a decreasing number of repetitions in a pyramid 
211	fashion until a target load is reached with about 3-4 repetitions. A partner immediately removes 5-10 kg and the 
212	athlete exercises to failure. Another 5-10 kg is removed at this point and the athlete continues again to failure. 
213	This process is usually continued until the starting weight or less is reachcd. This method is commonly used for 
214	muscle endurance and definition training. If the rising pyramid allows the athlete to reach a 1 RM or 2RM with no 
215	more than 6 repetitions for any set, then stripping offers a logical way of developing strength and muscle 
216	endurance, since the use of higher repetition sets is too fatiguing to enable one to reach a true 1RM.
217	Pyramid Method This method characteristically involves performing 4-5 sets of an exercisc where the load is 
218	progressively increased and the number of repetitions decreased with each set. A typical sub-maximal example
219	397
220	
221	=================== PDF 409
222	SUPERTRAINING
223	would be 10 x 70% .IRM, 8 x 80% .IRM, 6 x 85% .IRM, 4 x 90%.IRM, whereas a maximal strength example 
224	would be 6 x 85% .IRM, 4 x 90% .IRM, 2 x 97% .IRM, 1 x 100%.IRM (values derived from the equations 
225	associated with Fig 1.9). The rest interval between sets is 2-6 minutes, depending on the load used, the aim of the 
226	pyramid and the number of the set (the rest increases with load).
227	One may distinguish between three different types of pyramiding: load pyramiding (the method just described), 
228	repetition pyramiding, in which the number o f repetitions with a fixed load is increased by one or two repetitions 
229	per set (e.g. from an initial 4 to a maximum of 10), and rest pyramiding, in which the interval between sets with a 
230	given load is progressively decreased. In the last case it is unusual to increase the load simultaneously; if done, the 
231	increments are kept small (2.5-5 kg). Other training methods which involve some form o f pyramiding are the 
232	DeLorme Method (see 5.2.1) and APRE (see 5.2.2). Pyramiding is rarely used by serious athletes today; they 
233	find it more beneficial to progress rapidly to the main training load and performing higher repetition work on the 
234	way down from a maximum, if absolutely necessary.
235	Reverse Pyramid Method This method usually requires the athlete to pyramid to a final set with a particular 
236	number of repetitions, then to work down the pyramid in reverse order using the same number of repetitions for 
237	each load that was used previously in working upwards. It is very similar to the stripping method, but does not 
238	require the athlete to exercise to failure as the load decreases with each set.
239	Interval Training Methods As in track athletics, the primary aim o f interval training is generally to develop 
240	strength-cndurance by means of systematically alternating work and recovery phases. The duration of the rest 
241	(preferably active rest) periods is insufficient to permit full recovery, so that the athlete is forced to cope with 
242	increasing exhaustion and thereby develop muscular endurance. Because o f increasing fatigue and the greater 
243	likelihood of injury under such conditions, exercises that require high levels o f skill are not recommended. It 
244	should be noted that much weightlifting and powerlifting training relies on a specific form of interval resistance 
245	training, namely the use of single repetitions of near-maximal weights with a few seconds of rest between 
246	repetitions. Thus, one may distinguish between two broad categories of interval resistance training: one to 
247	increase strength or power and the other to increase endurance. With reference to the latter, there are two basic 
248	endurance interval weight training methods: extensive and intensive.
249	• 
250	Extensive Interval Training increases medium duration strength-endurance with loads of low to average 
251	intensity, as well as the capacity to recover after such activity. Since the training load is less than 40% of 
252	maximum, arterial blood flow is not restricted by muscle contraction and 'aerobic' energy processes 
253	predominate over 'anaerobic' processes. Training loads are between 30-40% of IRM for 5-6 sets of 20-30 
254	repetitions per set, with rest intervals o f 1-2 minutes. The most appropriate exercises involve the larger 
255	muscle groups such as the quadriceps, glutei, pectorals and erector spinae; exercises such as bicep curls, calf 
256	raises and tricep push-downs play a minimal role in elevating the heart rate to the level recommended for 
257	aerobic conditioning, e.g. 75% of (220-Age). Specially designed circuit training programmes can meet the 
258	requirements for extensive interval training.
259	• Intensive Interval Training increases short-duration strength-endurance with medium to fairly high intensity 
260	loads and the capacity to recover after such activity. The higher training loads inhibit arterial blood flow and 
261	anaerobic energy processes predominate over aerobic processes. Training loads are 50-60% of I RM for 3*6 
262	sets, where each set is performed to failure and rest intervals last 10-90 seconds, depending on the exercises, 
263	load, the athlete's level o f special fitness and duration of loading. The high loading intensity can readily in­
264	crease heart rates to over 180 beats/min. Special circuits may be designed to offer this type of training, in 
265	which case the rest interval between successive circuits is 1-3 minutes.
266	Zone Training This refers to training a specific body zone in a particular workout session so that an entire body 
267	training regime using this method must be spread over several sessions or days. Split routines constitute one 
268	variation of this method.
269	Cluster Training This term is applied to another form of interval training that requires one to perform one or 
270	more repetitions with a 10-20 second interval between each repetition or cluster of repetitions in an extended set. 
271	Characteristically, the minimum load used is one's 5RM and 4-6 sets are performed. As is the case with general 
272	interval training, there are two forms of clustering: extensive and intensive. 
273	Extensive clustering involves 4-6 
274	repetitions with one's 4-6RM, with 10 second rest intervals between each cluster. It may also be performed in a 
275	way which is similar to stripping: after each set, the load is decreased by 10-20% and a 10 second rest is taken
276	398
277	
278	=================== PDF 410
279	SUPERTRAINING
280	before the next set. Intensive clustering involves 4-6 sets of only one repetition with 75-90% of 1 RM, with about 
281	a 20 second rest between repetitions for 4-6 repetitions.
282	Continuous Tension Sets This term is applied to any set in which each repetition is done smoothly without 
283	ballistic bounce, cheating or significant pause at either end of the motion. Characteristically, the movements are 
284	executed fairly slowly without the joints locking completely at any stage of the exercise. Movements done in 
285	circular patterns such as cycling or arm ergometry produce continuous tension naturally and easily.
286	Progressive Segmental Training This method involves dividing the range o f movement into 2-4 segments, then 
287	performing 3-7 repetitions in each successive segment. A popular form of this system in bodybuilding is known 
288	as Twenty-Ones\ which consists of 7 repetitions done over three segments o f a given exercise. Thus, in the case 
289	of bicep curls, the bar is lifted for 7 repetitions over the first third of the range, 7 repetitions over the middle third 
290	and 7 repetitions over the final third to the shoulders (or frequently, over the full range of movement).
291	Some weightlifters, such as the Russian midheavyweight, Rigert, used this method for training the pull in the 
292	dean and the snatch. For instance, in the case of the clean pull, the bar first was raised to just below the knees for 
293	1*3 repetitions, next the bar was moved for 1-3 repetitions between this point and mid-thigh, and, finally, 1-3 
294	repetitions were performed between mid-thigh and waist level with full shoulder shrug and extension onto the 
295	toes. Frequently, the set was completed with a full clean pull from the ground.
296	One bodybuilding variation is to exercise various segments o f range in a different or random order or pattern 
297	every set or workout to minimise the possibility of early accommodation to a predictable regime, which can 
298	diminish the training effect. For want of a better term, this method might be referred to as Random Segmental 
299	Training.
300	Hybrid Training This method of complexing various movements in a given exercise refers to exercise in which 
301	each repetition consists of two or more separate movements between the starting and end points. 
302	The 
303	weightlifting clean-and-jerk, which combines a pull from the ground, with a front squat, followed by a thrust 
304	overhead, is probably the best known hybrid exercise. Not only docs this lift consist of these discrete movements, 
305	but it also exercises an extensive variety of muscle groups, including the quadriceps, glutei, erector spinae, trapezii, 
306	hamstrings, deltoids, gastrocnemius and triceps. It is doubtful if any manoeuvre in any other sport rivals the 
307	clcan-and-jerk or clean-and-push-press in recruiting maximal or near maximal contraction in so many muscle 
308	groups in such a short time (Table 3.12 gives the actual energy expenditure for the major lifts; the clean-and-jerk 
309	costs over 60kJ per maximal lift, higher than all other lifts). This is due to the fact that all hybrid exercises 
310	involves more joints of the body moving through a greater number of degrees of freedom. Their value in producing 
311	a more concentrated form of circuit training then becomes obvious. Instead of doing three separate exercises at 
312	three different stations, one can do all of them in a single repetition or at a single station.
313	The hybrid method refers not only to a single repetition consisting of several different movements, but also to 
314	the hybrid set, which comprises a different movement for each repetition of the set.
315	Examples of hybrid repetitions are:
316	• Barbell or DB curl + overhead standing press (normal or reverse grip)
317	• Back or front squat + press (or push press or jerk)
318	• Squat + good morning
319	• DB lateral raises (palms pronated) + upright row
320	• DB bench press + bent elbow pullovers (or flyes)
321	Examples of hybrid sets are:
322	• Reps 1-5: DB press; Reps 6-10: DB curl; Reps 11-15: Lateral raises
323	• Reps 1-5: narrow-grip bench press; Reps 6-10: wide-grip bench press
324	• Reps 1-5: squats; Reps 6-15: calf raises
325	• Reps 1-5: squats; Reps 6-10: overhead press or push press
326	• Reps 1-5: DB bench press; Reps 6-10: bcnt-elbow DB flyes; Reps 11-15: bent-elbow DB pullovers.
327	It is unnecessary to do the same number of repetitions for each movement in a hybrid set. For instance, one could 
328	perform the following set:
329	399
330	
331	=================== PDF 411
332	SUPERTRAINING
333	Reps 1-3: Power clean from the hang (3 reps); Reps 4-8: front squat (5 reps); Reps 9-10: push press (2 reps). 
334	According to the recording convention in 6.6.2, this routine may be written down as follows for a bar loaded to 
335	80kg, for a set of 3 repetitions:
336	Power clean / front squat / push press : —^ —
337	3+5+2
338	Numerous hybrid repetitions and sets may be devised by the inventive coach, as long as ccrtain guidelines are 
339	followed to avoid injury for this demanding type o f training. 
340	The load must be selected so that it can be 
341	performed without excessive strain in the weakest movement of the hybrid. The order of movements should 
342	always be arranged to permit their safe and controlled execution without causing exhaustion, impaired technique or 
343	overloading. A much larger selection of hybrid exercises commonly used in heavy strength training is provided in 
344	the following chaptcr (Ch 8.4).
345	Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT) Discussed periodically in earlier chapters, this method refers to the 
346	process o f deliberately trying to accelerate the bar throughout the concentric phase of the movement, instead of 
347	allowing the load alone to determine how one should move. According to Newton’s Second Law (F * m.a), an 
348	increase in acceleration will increase muscle tension and enhance the training effect of any resistance exercise. 
349	Similarly, the training effect of an entire movement may also be enhanced by deliberately slowing the motion down 
350	during its eccentric phase, a process which may be termed Compensatory Deceleration Training. If one combines 
351	both of these deliberate control approaches, the resulting method may be called Compensatory Action Training. 
352	However, the original name of Compensatory Acceleration Training still may be retained, because acceleration in 
353	biomechanics may be either positive or negative (i.e. deceleration).
354	Other Methods Besides the methods described above, several other training variants were discussed elsewhere in 
355	detail, such as the DeLorme, McCloy and Oxford (5.2.1), dynamic APRE (5.2.2), isokinetics (4.2.6), and 
356	electrostimuiation (4.2.1) methods.
357	Reactive Methods
358	Reactive methods are intended to develop power and explosive strength by imposing specific demands on nervous 
359	processes. One of these methods, namely plyometrics, has already been discussed at length earlier (5.2.4). This 
360	category is completed by adding another group of reactive methods, known as Contrast Methods:
361	Load release This method involves executing an exercise with an added load, then releasing the load suddenly 
362	during the lift, so that the contrast in stimulus received by the nervous system produces a rapid acceleration. For 
363	example, an athlete may execute a repetition of'dips' or pullups as powerfully as possible with a load grasped 
364	between the legs, then release the load early during the next repetition and accelerate rapidly upwards for the 
365	remainder of the movement. 
366	The stripping method discussed earlier in this section, offers a non-explosive 
367	variation of this method. As mentioned earlier, the contrast method also refers to the sudden release of a 
368	parachute attached with a harness to an athlete running, swimming or cycling at high speed.
369	Pneumatics This method is much the same as the preceding contrast method. Instead of exercising with an added 
370	weight, one trains on a machine which offers resistance with compressed air. This system enables the air pressure 
371	to be quickly increased or decreased at any stage o f a movement at the touch of a button, thereby enabling the 
372	athlete to decrease the resistance fairly rapidly, though not as rapidly as with the load release method. In the 
373	USA, the Keiser company makes a well-known range of these pneumatic machines.
374	Heavy-Light Set This method involves performing a low repetition heavy set, decreasing the load by about 20%, 
375	taking a rest of 10-20 seconds, then executing the lighter set as rapidly as possible for 3-5 repetitions. The 
376	nervous system remains briefly adapted to the heavy load if the rest interval is brief and the muscles are 
377	temporarily able to operate in this super-stimulated condition to produce a very powerful and rapid contraction 
378	with the lightened load.
379	Static-Dynamic Method This method exploits the fact that preliminary isometric tension using one or very few 
380	repetitions can increase the dynamic strength and explosive strength of a subsequent action, as a result of the 
381	after-effect phenomenon (see 3.3.1 and 3.4.2). The magnitude of the after-effect is influenced by many factors, 
382	including the duration of static loading, muscular fatigue and the interval between the static stimulus and the 
383	subsequent action.
384	400
385	
386	=================== PDF 412
387	SUPERTRAINING
388	There arc a host of different bodybuilding methods that offer interesting and innovative ways of training the body, 
389	predominantly for achieving greater muscle hypertrophy. These are not discussed at length here because they arc 
390	of minimal significance for developing most of the specific functional types of strength fitness required in 
391	competitive sport. Only a brief summary of some of the better known bodybuilding methods is given to provide 
392	the coach with working definitions of methods that he may wish to apply in an hypertrophy phase for a given 
393	athlete. The intention of most of these methods is to offer a novel variation to shock the body or particular 
394	muscle group out of any prevailing state of habituation or stagnation and thereby encourage adaptation at a higher 
395	level of performance.
396	Strict Sets Probably the best known of all types of classical bodybuilding training is the strict set which refers to 
397	any set that is done according to precise form without the use of momentum, any deviation from the prescribed 
398	kinesiological pattern or any form o f’cheating'. It is advisable that all beginners leam first with strict sets to create 
399	the appropriate neuromuscular patterns of control before moving to other variations.
400	Muscle Priority Sets These are sets which arc organised so that the most undeveloped muscle groups are exercised 
401	first in a workout to ensure that the athlete has sufficient energy and motivation to devote to developing the 
402	relevant muscles.
403	Major to Minor Muscle Sets This method entails exercising the muscles in a sequence that begins with the largest 
404	or most powerful muscles and progresses to the smaller or weaker muscles. Instructors often are taught that this 
405	is the most effective way to train and this is generally acceptable for the beginner in the general preparation phase, 
406	but it should not be stipulated as general principle for all training. There are many reasons to deviate from this 
407	order, such as to use pre-exhaustion training to develop stubborn muscles, to follow the muscle priority system 
408	given directly above, to facilitate recovery after heavy training o f the same muscles in a previous workout, to 
409	accommodate two or more workouts on one day, and to obey principles of Junctional priority discussed earlier in 
410	this text (i.e. technical skills > speed-strength > strength-speed > strength > strength-endurance > general 
411	endurance).
412	Alternating Sets This involves alternating sets of exercises for different regions of the body to achieve specific 
413	training goals. There are several ways in which alternation is used: major-minor muscle (staggered) sets, upper- 
414	lower body sets and agonist-antagonist sets. Staggered Sets are supersets which alternate one set for major muscle 
415	groups with a set for minor muscles in an attempt to gainfully use the long rest intervals between each set of 
416	exercises for the major muscles. Upper-Lower Body Sets, sometimes inappropriately called peripheral heart action 
417	(PHA) sets, alternate a set for the upper body with one for the lower body. This switch to heavy activation of 
418	one body part tends to promote reflexive relaxation of another distant body part, a process first described by 
419	Setchinov in the early 1900s. Proponents of the PHA concept believe that this system avoids engorging one 
420	muscle part with blood and encourages the development of circulatory fitness. The fact is that all human resisted 
421	movement and not just PHA encourages peripheral circulation and PHA offers no superior cardio-circulatory 
422	benefits compared with other systems of resistance training. Agonist-Antagonist Setscxcrcise agonist muscles of 
423	one joint with the antagonistic muscles of the same joint (e.g. triceps followed by biceps), either in the form of 
424	supersets or as successive sets.
425	Tempo Changing Sets These sets involve changing the tempo (or pace) of an exercise during each set, so that 
426	either one repetition may be performed faster or slower than other repetitions, or the duration of the concentric, 
427	isometric and eccentric phases of a single repetition may be changed relative to one another during each repetition. 
428	This variation, like any other forms that stimulate the body in an unexpected way, may be of value in preventing 
429	habituation and stagnation (see Fig 1.32) after long periods of training.
430	Diminishing Sets This method entails trying to perform a very large number of repetitions (usually 100) in as few 
431	sets as possible with the same load, with a minimal rest period between sets, for example 30-25-20-15-10. The 
432	newcomer to this method may have to use as many as 10-12 sets, but the ultimate aim is to decrease the number 
433	of necessary sets rather than to increase the load. When one is capable of executing the 100 repetitions in 4-5 sets, 
434	then the load should be increased for the next workout.
435	Rep Pausing Sets This method entails taking a short rest break during the execution of a set to facilitate recovery, 
436	diminish the pain of effort or overcome any loss of motivation before completing the remaining repetitions.
437	Miscellaneous M ethods
438	401
439	
440	=================== PDF 413
441	SUPERTRAINING
442	Holding Sets This method involves holding the weight statically at a given point during or at the end of a 
443	movement to isometrically strengthen the muscles, the tendons and joint capsules, as well as improving overall 
444	balance in certain lifts above the head (e.g. the clean or press).
445	Cumulative Sets This method entails beginning with a set of one repetition and adding on one repetition to each 
446	set until a final set to failure is reached. Usually this method employs one's 10RM, with 10 second rest intervals 
447	between each set.
448	Peak Contraction Sets This method requires you to complete each repetition at the point of maximal muscle 
449	contraction (see Figs 2.8, 2.9) and not at the end of range when the force has already diminished significantly. 
450	Usually, one consciously attempts to increase muscle tension in that position by means o f intense isometric or 
451	quasi-isometric contraction.
452	Methods for Overcoming Barriers
453	The inevitable reaching of a ‘sticking point’ in training is one of single most frustrating experiences in the life of 
454	any athlete. It may lead to loss of form, loss of interest, decrease in motivation, the unnecessary or premature 
455	reliance on anabolic substances, an endless search for plausible ergogenic aids, injury or even the end of one’s 
456	sporting career. 
457	Therefore, it is useful to become aware of a repertoire of various strategies which may 
458	implemented to help one break through these performance barriers. 
459	Among some of the methods are the 
460	following:
461	1. Attempt to increase the number of repetitions with near maximal loads. Thus, for example, try to increase
462	your 2RM to a 3RM or your 3RM to a 5RM
463	2. Decrease your higher repetition training and include more IRM, 2RM or 3RM training
464	3. Use CAT (Compensatory Acceleration Training) methods with lighter loads
465	4. Increase loads by unfamiliar increments, since sticking points often relate to the numerical value of the load
466	which one associates with one’s current 1 RM. Thus, of increasing to one’s 1 RM of 100kg via a succession 
467	of sets like 80 - 90 - 95 - 100kg, change the sequence to sets of 80 - 92.5 - 97.5 - 102.5kg.
468	5. Change your warm-up strategy. Instead of wasting energy on prolonged repetitions or sets, devise a less
469	demanding warm-up which conserves energy for the heaviest lifts.
470	6. Increase the increment in loads used in successive sets, provided that warm-up has been adequate. Thus,
471	instead of using successive sets of 60 - 70 - 80 - 90 - 100kg, change to a sequence such as 60 - 80 - 100kg, 
472	where you may perform some more repetitions with 60kg, if you feel that a longer warm-up suits you 
473	better. To compensate for any decrease in overall volume of loading, you may add a few heavier sets or 
474	plateau with another few sets at 100kg.
475	7. If you uses pyramids, use fewer repetition sets to reach your maximum, then do your repetition work during
476	a reverse pyramid down from your maximum. This can be especially useful if you wish to concurrently 
477	work on strength and hypertrophy.
478	8. Add minimal increments near your attempts with your IRM or reps to failure training. This requires the use
479	of very light weights of 0.5 - 1.25kg, which may be bought from suppliers of competitive lifting equipment 
480	or specially made by engineering shops. When one adds these weights, you do not count the extra load; you 
481	simply train as if the load is the same as if these small increments were not there. Sometimes, you may even 
482	sneak these weights between the larger plates if you wish to help a colleague break through some largely 
483	psychological barrier.
484	9. Use any of the contrast training methods discussed earlier.
485	10. Change some aspects of your typical training session, such as the order or duration of various exercises.
486	11. Use supramaximal adaptation training (SAT) methods, which entail actions like taking a load which is 
487	significantly heavier than your IRM off a rack and supporting it, executing ‘lock-outs’ at the end of range, or 
488	performing small end-of-rangc repetitions.
489	12. Alter or improve your technique in problematic exercises. Sometimes your sticking point is due to imperfect 
490	technique, so that a skilled coach, together with video analysis of your movements, can help you carry out 
491	the necessary changes. It is unwise to attempt any changes in technique close to any competitions, unless 
492	there is something seriously inefficient or unsafe in your existing technique.
493	402
494	
495	=================== PDF 414
496	SUPERTRAINING
497	13. Ensure that your rest periods between sets or repetitions are optimal. Rests which are either too short or too 
498	long both may disrupt your ability to perform optimally, so it is essential that you experiment or apply 
499	appropriate tests (e.g. heart rate, motor control) to 
500	determine rest intervals which best suit you. In 
501	competition, however, the rules or number of competitors may not allow you optimal rest between attempts, 
502	so that it is vital that you train with different rest intervals to leam to cope with such situations.
503	14. Take a short break from your regular training to overcome mental stagnation and facilitate restoration.
504	15. Use fewer exercises in your workout
505	16. Include more variation in your workout.
506	17. Use shorter, more frequent workouts
507	18. Subdivide your workouts into rational modules of a few exercises, then do two or more modules per day.
508	20. Use ballistic methods to move through a sticking point in an exercise.
509	21. Perform loaded isometric holds at crucial points
510	22. Include formal restoration in your training programme, if you do not already do so
511	23. Implement appropriate mental strategies by consulting qualified specialists
512	24. Take a short break from the problem exercise or event
513	25. Implement a basic periodisation programme or at least an portion of one, if you arc not already following one.
514	26. Use assistance exercises to strengthen areas of weakness in the problem exercise
515	27. Use ‘forced repetitions* with the aid of a training partner (details given earlier in Ch 7.1)
516	28. Use variable resistance methods such as free weights combined with elastics or chains.
517	Concluding Remarks
518	The above summary by no means exhausts the repertoire of methods and variations of resistance training that is 
519	used in resistance training, but it serves as a rapid reference for the major methods which are most frequently used 
520	in the training of high-level athletes. It intentionally docs not address several other methods quoted or ’invented' 
521	by writers in popular bodybuilding magazines, simply because they differ only in name and a few minor details 
522	from existing methods and do not constitute any major new contribution to the field of strength training.
523	In applying any of the methods discussed in this section, it is essential that the detailed information 
524	conccming their mechanisms and use given in earlier chapters be consulted in conjunction with the above 
525	summaries. It should never be forgotten that no methods operate in isolation of one another; each method has 
526	immediate and delayed training effects which have significant effects on other methods that follow hours, days or 
527	even weeks later (e.g. sec 3.3.1, 3.4, 5.3, 5.4 and all Ch 6).
528	The next section examines a physical conditioning system which is widely used in physiotherapy, but is 
529	rarely regarded as a means of training the normal athlete, except occasionally in the specific situation of improving 
530	flexibility. This system, known by the somewhat daunting name of Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation 
531	or, PNF for short, however, can offer a highly comprehensive strength training system that encompasses and 
532	augments many of the methods and techniques of resistance exercise.
533	7.2 PNF as a Training System
534	Strength training is often regarded as a discipline confined largely to the gymnasium or sports field. 
535	Unfortunately, this can obscure the fact that it can and does appear in other situations which have little direct 
536	connection with sport.
537	In particular, PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) contains many useful techniques which can 
538	play an important role in the strength training of athletes. It is one of the aims of this section to show that PNF is 
539	a comprehensive conditioning system which includes not only many of the principles already covered in this 
540	book, but also adds insights which complement these principles.
541	PNF is invariably regarded by conditioning coaches as a special type of sophisticated stretching, alongside 
542	static, ballistic and passive stretching. PNF is far more than just another stretching technique; it is actually an 
543	entire system o f therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures for rehabilitating 
544	patients suffering from various musculoskeletal injuries or disabilities. Stretching constitutes but one o f many 
545	aspects of the full repertoire of PNF methods, yet even those enlightened coaches who use PNF extol only its 
546	virtues as a stretching system.
547	403
548

SUPERTRAINING
STRENGTH TRAINING 
METHODS
The preceding chapters have extracted many of the principles, means and methods of strength training, but it 
cannot be claimed that the task of presenting an exhaustive holistic system is complete. Many further steps have 
to be taken to produce an integrated system of strength conditioning, guided by thorough research and examination 
of practical methods implemented by anyone for whom the quest for strength is important. As mentioned in 
Chapter 1, the sources of information on the art and science of strength training are the following:
• Weighdifting and Powerlifting
• Bodybuilding
• Supplementary resistance training
• Physical therapy
• Scientific research
The weight training gymnasium, whose origins lie in Grecian and pre-Grecian times, has provided a natural 
laboratory replete with subjects who have used weightlifting, powerlifting or bodybuilding to explore the 
boundaries of human muscle development for their specific purposes. It should not be surprising that this should 
have becomc a fertile setting for experientially discovering strength training methods. Weightlifters have become 
experts at developing explosive strength and skill, bodybuilders at producing massive hypertrophy and low body 
(at, and powerliftcrs at developing slow speed and maximal isometric strength.
Only in recent years, has science begun to investigate seriously the foundations, validity and scope of the 
vast amount of practical information gathered by several generations of adherents of the 'Iron Game'. 
Consequently, resistance training is rapidly losing stigmas such as 'slowing one down', 'making one muscle-bound', 
decreasing flexibility’ and 'causing back injury'. 
Scientists entering the field of strength training have been 
surprised at the enormous body of knowledge accumulated by competitors in the strength sports and have been 
devoting their ingenuity to devise reproducible experiments to investigate all training methods for different 
subjects at different stages of fitness. Their research has also led them to add to this encyclopaedia of strength 
training techniques various methods taken from other sports requiring the display of different types of strength 
fitness, in particular, track-and-field. Thus, plyometrics, circuit training and cross training became recognised as 
valuable training methods.
Few coaches have realised that physiotherapy also offers many useful adjunct methods of musculoskeletal 
and neuromuscular training, such as electrostimuiation, accelerated recuperation and PNF (proprioceptive 
neuromuscular facilitation). Because of the broad scope of training offered by PNF, this system is discussed in 
detail later in this chapter.
As has been stressed throughout this text, all strength training depends on two dominant factors (e.g. see Ch 
I), namely structural conditioning and functional (central nervous and neuromuscular) conditioning. 
Thus, 
strength training may be categorised according to its 
major structural and functional aims relative to the 
importance of nervous system training methods (Fig 7.1). The numerous methods and techniques of training may 
then be added hierarchically below each of these major aims.
It is tempting to attempt to devise a single extensive flowchart to categorise and interrelate all of the better 
known methods of resistance training, but the extent of overlap between the different methods makes the final 
result logically tedious, unattractive and largely unusable. Instead, it is simpler to organise the different methods 
as a loosely interconnected array of columns and rows, showing only some of the more obvious relationships (Fig 
7.2). The merit of this type of chart is that it enables one to see at a glance the variety o f many of the methods 
which were discussed in previous chapters. Where necessary, any terminology and methods that did not appear 
explicitly in the book are described later, so as to furnish the reader with a compendium of methods for practical 
application.
In using the summary depicted in Figure 7.2, it is important to note that some of the training methods may be 
used to achieve several different aims by altering variables such as the load, number of repetitions and rest 
intervals. For example, pyramiding should not be regarded merely as a bodybuilding method, because it may also

be used in the earlier preparatory stages to meet several general training aims such as increased muscic 
hypertrophy, strength and endurance, depending on the load and number o f repetitions (which are inversely 
related). Therefore, pyramiding has been classified separately to show the different forms of pyramiding that arc 
commonly used in the broad field of strength training.
Figure 7.1 Broad classification o f the major aims o f strength training. The development of power refers to the qualities of strength- 
speed and speed-strength, as discussed throughout this text.
The method of quasi-isometrics occurs as a natural consequence of training with near-maximal loads, since it is 
impossible to move any heavy load at high speed without the use of ballistic techniques. However, there is a 
discrete method of quasi-isometrics (nowadays popularised in bodybuilding circles as the superslow method), 
which entails performing very slow controlled repetitions with even moderately heavy or lighter loads. In this 
case the athlete chooses to move the load slowly; with heavier weights he has no option but to move slowly.
Flexibility training has not been elaborated upon beyond its broad subdivision into static, active and other 
forms, since details o f its development were discussed earlier in depth (3.5). It should also be noted that several 
of the other training methods with heavy resistance used over a full range of movement constitute very effective 
means of active stretching.
In organising any training programme, it should always be remembered that great emphasis should be placed 
on increasing the mass and strength of the connective tissues, such as the tendons, ligaments, cartilages and joint 
capsules, particularly during the early stages of training and transition phases to levels of higher competitive 
intensity (see 1.6.2). An essential part o f the general preparatory phase of all training is also low intensity, 
prolonged cyclical activity to enhance cardiovascular and circulatory processes, as well as capillarisation in all the 
relevant muscle groups. This same type of activity can also play a useful role in restoration between intensive 
training sessions and phases.
7.1 Bodybuilding and O ther Strength Training Methods
The selection of any resistance training method to achieve a desired training effect may be determined on the basis 
of competitive experience and research into the phenomena of strength, adaptation, specificity and 
supercompensation, which were discussed in great detail in the preceding chapters. 
The various resistance 
training methods are categorised according to the general scheme presented in Figure 7.2.
In doing so, it is important to appreciate that certain methods classified under one heading may sometimes 
also be used to produce effects falling under other headings. 
For instance, cheating and restricted range 
repetitions, although classified as supramaximal methods, may also be used submaximally or circamaximally. It 
the role of the coach to choose a given method according to the intended training goal and adapt it accordingly. In 
this regard. Table 1.1, which was based largely on the practical experience o f generations of bodybuilders and 
weightlifters, may serve as an initial guide to be viewed in the light of the scheme depicted in Figure 7.1.
The choice between a focus on hypertrophy or nervous system training may be based on performance in tests 
of explosive strength and speed-strength (e.g. vertical jump), as well as on the magnitude of the strength deficit 
discussed early in Chapter 1. If this deficit at any stage is large, then it would be appropriate to concentrate more 
on weightlifting and reactive methods, whereas, if the deficit is small, submaximal bodybuilding methods should be 
relied upon.

Maximal Methods
Weightlifting Method This method is characterised by single repetition explosive sets or low repetition sets (2-3 
reps), in which each repetition is separated from the next by a short rest period (1-5 minutes, depending on how 
close the load is to a I RM). Sometimes this method is referred to as the interval set method. This IRM set with 
optimal recovery intervals between sets has been adopted by bodybuilders as the rest-pause method, which also

The load is carefully controlled until the end position is reached, when the partner lifts it through the concentric

muscle soreness than most other methods and should not be used too frequently. Its dangers can be reduced by 
selecting the load carefully and avoiding sudden changes in movement velocity or trajectory.
Supramaximal Methods
Forced repetitions This method involves working to failure with a given load, then executing a few more 
repetitions with the aid of a training partner, who provides the minimal assistance necessary to enable the 
concentric phase to be completed successfully. The eccentric phase of the exercise is carried out without help.
Restricted range repetitions The athlete chooses a load which is heavier than the maximum that he can use for the 
complete cycle of the exercise, then he performs a few small range concentric-eccentric repetitions near his 
strongest region of action for that exercise. If these repetitions are performed at the end of a normal 5-8 
repetition concentric-eccentric set to the point where the muscles begin to 'bum', this method is known as burning 
reps to the body-building fraternity. One may also execute concentric or eccentric restricted range movements 
with the aid of a partner (as with the forced repetition method).
In weightlifting or powerlifting, an exercise may be performed over a specific range with a load greater than 
one's capability for the full movement to rectify any deficit of strength in that region. Typical examples are 
pulling exercises around knee-to-lower thigh level and squats or bench presses in the range of one's 'sticking point'. 
Power racks or plinths are commonly to secure the weight in a given starting position. Restricted range exercises 
may also be done with maximal or submaximal loads, depending on one's training purpose.
Cheating This method involves the use of momentum, bouncing of the bar against the body, swaying the body, 
using accessory muscles or otherwise completing an exercise by deviating from its traditionally strict form. This 
may be done to complete any exercise with weights heavier than one's I RM or at the end of a fairly heavy set 
which has taken one to the point of failure. There are recommended safe ways of cheating and these must be 
followed religiously if injury is to be avoided.
Ballistics This method is sometimes regarded as a form o f cheating and involves lowering or dropping a weight 
rapidly to recruit the myotatic stretch reflex or exploit the stored elastic energy in the tendons and other 
connective tissues. Although this method is classified as supramaximal, the training load is not necessarily 
supramaximal; rather, it is the resulting muscle tension that reaches this level of intensity.
Circa-maximal Methods
These methods, which may involve all of the preceding methods, implicate training with loads that are close to 
one's IRM (characteristically about 90-97.5% of IRM). The main difference between maximal and circa-maximal 
methods is that the latter may be performed with several successive repetitions without a prolonged rest interval.
Submaximal Methods
Submaximal or repetition methods characteristically involve training with loads of about 60-80% of one's IRM to 
the point of failure on the last set. 
The smaller loads enable the exercise to be performed with multiple 
repetitions, mainly for bodybuilding reasons such as hypertrophy or muscle definition.

I Classical Bodybuilding Regime This is one of the best known elementary bodybuilding methods and involves 
3 to 5 sets of 8-10 repetitions with the same load, allowing a rest interval of 2-5 minutes between sets. This may 
also be regarded as a particular case of the plateau system of training with an unchanging load. Another classical 
method involves increasing the load with each set so that the athlete is compelled to progressively decrease the 
number of repetitions from 10 in the first set to 4-5 repetitions in the last set. The rest interval increases as the 
load increases. This is a typical form of the pyramid system of training.
B. Extensive Bodybuilding Regime This high volume method involves 3-5 sets of 15-20 repetitions with a load of 
about 60-70%. The rest interval between sets is 2-3 minutes, increasing with increase in load from set to set.
C Intensive Bodybuilding Regime This high intensity method involves 3-5 sets of 5-8 repetitions with a load of 
80-90% (see Figs 1.8 and 1.9). The heavier loads mean that the rest interval between sets should be between 2-5 
minutes, increasing with increase in load.
Each of the preceding regimes may use the following methods which have been defined earlier: forced repetitions, 
cheating, eccentrics (negatives), burning repetitions and ballistics. 
In addition, the following methods are 
popularly used:
Supersets A superset usually consists of two separate exercises in which the athlete performs set 1 of exercise 1, 
moves immediately to set 1 of exercise 2, then performs set 2 of exercise 1, set 2 of exercise 2 and so on until the 
chosen number of sets is completed. Since supersets are not intended to develop strength, the athlete allows little 
or no rest between sets. Sometimes supersets involve more than two exercises, in which case it is probably more 
appropriate to refer to the extended method as multi-setting. A well-known type of multi-set is the giant set, 
which comprises 4-6 different exercises performed in a mini-circuit.
Pre-exhaustion This involves performing a single-joint exercise which preferentially exhausts one of the muscle 
groups that will be used in the following multi-joint exercisc. Not only docs this work the one muscle group 
intensively, but it compels other muscles to act strongly as accessory muscles. For example, if supine dumbbell 
flyes are performed before a bench press, the pectoral and anterior deltoid muscles are pre-exhausted and the 
triceps are forced to bccome more vigorously involved.
Repetitions to Failure This method simply involves continuing the exercise until it is impossible to execute 
another repetition without assistance. It is often used for muscle endurance and definition training.
Split Routine This system involves dividing a routine into two distinct components, each of which trains a 
different body zone in successive workouts. For example, upper body exercises may be done on one day, 
followed by lower body exercises the next day. Another system may involve flexor and adductor training on one 
day, with extensor and abductor training on the next day. Sometimes, the advanced athlete may execute one part 
of the split early in the day and the other part later. A common weekly split routine prescribes split training on 
Monday-Tucsday, resting on Wednesday, more split training on Thursday-Friday, completed by a weekend of 
passive or active rest.
Plateau Method After a specific warmup with a light weight, the load remains constant for 3-4 sets (e.g. 50 x 10, 
70 x 6, 70 x 6, 70 x 6). This method is commonly used during the early stages of training novices or for 
transitional active rest phases after weeks of heavy training.
Step Method The number of repetitions is kept fixed, while the load is increased after each set until the prescribed 
number of repetitions can no longer be maintained (e.g. 60 x 3, 70 x 3, 80 x 3, 85 x 3).
Stripping (Descending Set) Method Some bodybuilders also use the name ‘Drop Sets’ for this method. 
It 
involves working progressively with an increasing load and a decreasing number of repetitions in a pyramid 
fashion until a target load is reached with about 3-4 repetitions. A partner immediately removes 5-10 kg and the 
athlete exercises to failure. Another 5-10 kg is removed at this point and the athlete continues again to failure. 
This process is usually continued until the starting weight or less is reachcd. This method is commonly used for 
muscle endurance and definition training. If the rising pyramid allows the athlete to reach a 1 RM or 2RM with no 
more than 6 repetitions for any set, then stripping offers a logical way of developing strength and muscle 
endurance, since the use of higher repetition sets is too fatiguing to enable one to reach a true 1RM.
Pyramid Method This method characteristically involves performing 4-5 sets of an exercisc where the load is 
progressively increased and the number of repetitions decreased with each set. A typical sub-maximal example

increments are kept small (2.5-5 kg). Other training methods which involve some form o f pyramiding are the 
DeLorme Method (see 5.2.1) and APRE (see 5.2.2). Pyramiding is rarely used by serious athletes today; they 
find it more beneficial to progress rapidly to the main training load and performing higher repetition work on the 
way down from a maximum, if absolutely necessary.
Reverse Pyramid Method This method usually requires the athlete to pyramid to a final set with a particular 
number of repetitions, then to work down the pyramid in reverse order using the same number of repetitions for 
each load that was used previously in working upwards. It is very similar to the stripping method, but does not 
require the athlete to exercise to failure as the load decreases with each set.
Interval Training Methods As in track athletics, the primary aim o f interval training is generally to develop 
strength-cndurance by means of systematically alternating work and recovery phases. The duration of the rest 
(preferably active rest) periods is insufficient to permit full recovery, so that the athlete is forced to cope with 
increasing exhaustion and thereby develop muscular endurance. Because o f increasing fatigue and the greater 
likelihood of injury under such conditions, exercises that require high levels o f skill are not recommended. It 
should be noted that much weightlifting and powerlifting training relies on a specific form of interval resistance 
training, namely the use of single repetitions of near-maximal weights with a few seconds of rest between 
repetitions. Thus, one may distinguish between two broad categories of interval resistance training: one to 
increase strength or power and the other to increase endurance. With reference to the latter, there are two basic 
endurance interval weight training methods: extensive and intensive.
• 
Extensive Interval Training increases medium duration strength-endurance with loads of low to average 
intensity, as well as the capacity to recover after such activity. Since the training load is less than 40% of 
maximum, arterial blood flow is not restricted by muscle contraction and 'aerobic' energy processes 
predominate over 'anaerobic' processes. Training loads are between 30-40% of IRM for 5-6 sets of 20-30 
repetitions per set, with rest intervals o f 1-2 minutes. The most appropriate exercises involve the larger 
muscle groups such as the quadriceps, glutei, pectorals and erector spinae; exercises such as bicep curls, calf 
raises and tricep push-downs play a minimal role in elevating the heart rate to the level recommended for 
aerobic conditioning, e.g. 75% of (220-Age). Specially designed circuit training programmes can meet the 
requirements for extensive interval training.
• Intensive Interval Training increases short-duration strength-endurance with medium to fairly high intensity 
loads and the capacity to recover after such activity. The higher training loads inhibit arterial blood flow and 
anaerobic energy processes predominate over aerobic processes. Training loads are 50-60% of I RM for 3*6 
sets, where each set is performed to failure and rest intervals last 10-90 seconds, depending on the exercises, 
load, the athlete's level o f special fitness and duration of loading. The high loading intensity can readily in­
crease heart rates to over 180 beats/min. Special circuits may be designed to offer this type of training, in 
which case the rest interval between successive circuits is 1-3 minutes.
Zone Training This refers to training a specific body zone in a particular workout session so that an entire body 
training regime using this method must be spread over several sessions or days. Split routines constitute one 
variation of this method.
Cluster Training This term is applied to another form of interval training that requires one to perform one or 
more repetitions with a 10-20 second interval between each repetition or cluster of repetitions in an extended set. 
Characteristically, the minimum load used is one's 5RM and 4-6 sets are performed. As is the case with general 
interval training, there are two forms of clustering: extensive and intensive. 
Extensive clustering involves 4-6 
repetitions with one's 4-6RM, with 10 second rest intervals between each cluster. It may also be performed in a 
way which is similar to stripping: after each set, the load is decreased by 10-20% and a 10 second rest is taken

weightlifting clean-and-jerk, which combines a pull from the ground, with a front squat, followed by a thrust

Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT) Discussed periodically in earlier chapters, this method refers to the 
process o f deliberately trying to accelerate the bar throughout the concentric phase of the movement, instead of 
allowing the load alone to determine how one should move. According to Newton’s Second Law (F * m.a), an 
increase in acceleration will increase muscle tension and enhance the training effect of any resistance exercise. 
Similarly, the training effect of an entire movement may also be enhanced by deliberately slowing the motion down 
during its eccentric phase, a process which may be termed Compensatory Deceleration Training. If one combines 
both of these deliberate control approaches, the resulting method may be called Compensatory Action Training. 
However, the original name of Compensatory Acceleration Training still may be retained, because acceleration in 
biomechanics may be either positive or negative (i.e. deceleration).

Reactive Methods
Reactive methods are intended to develop power and explosive strength by imposing specific demands on nervous 
processes. One of these methods, namely plyometrics, has already been discussed at length earlier (5.2.4). This 
category is completed by adding another group of reactive methods, known as Contrast Methods:
Load release This method involves executing an exercise with an added load, then releasing the load suddenly 
during the lift, so that the contrast in stimulus received by the nervous system produces a rapid acceleration. For 
example, an athlete may execute a repetition of'dips' or pullups as powerfully as possible with a load grasped 
between the legs, then release the load early during the next repetition and accelerate rapidly upwards for the 
remainder of the movement. 
The stripping method discussed earlier in this section, offers a non-explosive 
variation of this method. As mentioned earlier, the contrast method also refers to the sudden release of a 
parachute attached with a harness to an athlete running, swimming or cycling at high speed.
Pneumatics This method is much the same as the preceding contrast method. Instead of exercising with an added 
weight, one trains on a machine which offers resistance with compressed air. This system enables the air pressure 
to be quickly increased or decreased at any stage o f a movement at the touch of a button, thereby enabling the 
athlete to decrease the resistance fairly rapidly, though not as rapidly as with the load release method. In the 
USA, the Keiser company makes a well-known range of these pneumatic machines.
Heavy-Light Set This method involves performing a low repetition heavy set, decreasing the load by about 20%, 
taking a rest of 10-20 seconds, then executing the lighter set as rapidly as possible for 3-5 repetitions. The 
nervous system remains briefly adapted to the heavy load if the rest interval is brief and the muscles are 
temporarily able to operate in this super-stimulated condition to produce a very powerful and rapid contraction 
with the lightened load.
Static-Dynamic Method This method exploits the fact that preliminary isometric tension using one or very few 
repetitions can increase the dynamic strength and explosive strength of a subsequent action, as a result of the 
after-effect phenomenon (see 3.3.1 and 3.4.2). The magnitude of the after-effect is influenced by many factors, 
including the duration of static loading, muscular fatigue and the interval between the static stimulus and the 
subsequent action.
