There arc a host of different bodybuilding methods that offer interesting and innovative ways of training the body, 
predominantly for achieving greater muscle hypertrophy. These are not discussed at length here because they arc 
of minimal significance for developing most of the specific functional types of strength fitness required in 
competitive sport. Only a brief summary of some of the better known bodybuilding methods is given to provide 
the coach with working definitions of methods that he may wish to apply in an hypertrophy phase for a given 
athlete. The intention of most of these methods is to offer a novel variation to shock the body or particular 
muscle group out of any prevailing state of habituation or stagnation and thereby encourage adaptation at a higher 
level of performance.
Strict Sets Probably the best known of all types of classical bodybuilding training is the strict set which refers to 
any set that is done according to precise form without the use of momentum, any deviation from the prescribed 
kinesiological pattern or any form o f’cheating'. It is advisable that all beginners leam first with strict sets to create 
the appropriate neuromuscular patterns of control before moving to other variations.
Muscle Priority Sets These are sets which arc organised so that the most undeveloped muscle groups are exercised 
first in a workout to ensure that the athlete has sufficient energy and motivation to devote to developing the 
relevant muscles.
Major to Minor Muscle Sets This method entails exercising the muscles in a sequence that begins with the largest 
or most powerful muscles and progresses to the smaller or weaker muscles. Instructors often are taught that this 
is the most effective way to train and this is generally acceptable for the beginner in the general preparation phase, 
but it should not be stipulated as general principle for all training. There are many reasons to deviate from this 
order, such as to use pre-exhaustion training to develop stubborn muscles, to follow the muscle priority system 
given directly above, to facilitate recovery after heavy training o f the same muscles in a previous workout, to 
accommodate two or more workouts on one day, and to obey principles of Junctional priority discussed earlier in 
this text (i.e. technical skills > speed-strength > strength-speed > strength > strength-endurance > general 
endurance).
Alternating Sets This involves alternating sets of exercises for different regions of the body to achieve specific 
training goals. There are several ways in which alternation is used: major-minor muscle (staggered) sets, upper- 
lower body sets and agonist-antagonist sets. Staggered Sets are supersets which alternate one set for major muscle 
groups with a set for minor muscles in an attempt to gainfully use the long rest intervals between each set of 
exercises for the major muscles. Upper-Lower Body Sets, sometimes inappropriately called peripheral heart action 
(PHA) sets, alternate a set for the upper body with one for the lower body. This switch to heavy activation of 
one body part tends to promote reflexive relaxation of another distant body part, a process first described by 
Setchinov in the early 1900s. Proponents of the PHA concept believe that this system avoids engorging one 
muscle part with blood and encourages the development of circulatory fitness. The fact is that all human resisted 
movement and not just PHA encourages peripheral circulation and PHA offers no superior cardio-circulatory 
benefits compared with other systems of resistance training. Agonist-Antagonist Setscxcrcise agonist muscles of 
one joint with the antagonistic muscles of the same joint (e.g. triceps followed by biceps), either in the form of 
supersets or as successive sets.
Tempo Changing Sets These sets involve changing the tempo (or pace) of an exercise during each set, so that 
either one repetition may be performed faster or slower than other repetitions, or the duration of the concentric, 
isometric and eccentric phases of a single repetition may be changed relative to one another during each repetition. 
This variation, like any other forms that stimulate the body in an unexpected way, may be of value in preventing 
habituation and stagnation (see Fig 1.32) after long periods of training.
Diminishing Sets This method entails trying to perform a very large number of repetitions (usually 100) in as few 
sets as possible with the same load, with a minimal rest period between sets, for example 30-25-20-15-10. The 
newcomer to this method may have to use as many as 10-12 sets, but the ultimate aim is to decrease the number 
of necessary sets rather than to increase the load. When one is capable of executing the 100 repetitions in 4-5 sets, 
then the load should be increased for the next workout.
Rep Pausing Sets This method entails taking a short rest break during the execution of a set to facilitate recovery, 
diminish the pain of effort or overcome any loss of motivation before completing the remaining repetitions.

Holding Sets This method involves holding the weight statically at a given point during or at the end of a 
movement to isometrically strengthen the muscles, the tendons and joint capsules, as well as improving overall 
balance in certain lifts above the head (e.g. the clean or press).

Methods for Overcoming Barriers
The inevitable reaching of a ‘sticking point’ in training is one of single most frustrating experiences in the life of 
any athlete. It may lead to loss of form, loss of interest, decrease in motivation, the unnecessary or premature 
reliance on anabolic substances, an endless search for plausible ergogenic aids, injury or even the end of one’s 
sporting career. 
Therefore, it is useful to become aware of a repertoire of various strategies which may 
implemented to help one break through these performance barriers. 
Among some of the methods are the 
following:
1. Attempt to increase the number of repetitions with near maximal loads. Thus, for example, try to increase
your 2RM to a 3RM or your 3RM to a 5RM
2. Decrease your higher repetition training and include more IRM, 2RM or 3RM training
3. Use CAT (Compensatory Acceleration Training) methods with lighter loads
4. Increase loads by unfamiliar increments, since sticking points often relate to the numerical value of the load
which one associates with one’s current 1 RM. Thus, of increasing to one’s 1 RM of 100kg via a succession 
of sets like 80 - 90 - 95 - 100kg, change the sequence to sets of 80 - 92.5 - 97.5 - 102.5kg.
5. Change your warm-up strategy. Instead of wasting energy on prolonged repetitions or sets, devise a less
demanding warm-up which conserves energy for the heaviest lifts.
6. Increase the increment in loads used in successive sets, provided that warm-up has been adequate. Thus,
instead of using successive sets of 60 - 70 - 80 - 90 - 100kg, change to a sequence such as 60 - 80 - 100kg, 
where you may perform some more repetitions with 60kg, if you feel that a longer warm-up suits you 
better. To compensate for any decrease in overall volume of loading, you may add a few heavier sets or 
plateau with another few sets at 100kg.
7. If you uses pyramids, use fewer repetition sets to reach your maximum, then do your repetition work during
a reverse pyramid down from your maximum. This can be especially useful if you wish to concurrently 
work on strength and hypertrophy.
8. Add minimal increments near your attempts with your IRM or reps to failure training. This requires the use
of very light weights of 0.5 - 1.25kg, which may be bought from suppliers of competitive lifting equipment 
or specially made by engineering shops. When one adds these weights, you do not count the extra load; you 
simply train as if the load is the same as if these small increments were not there. Sometimes, you may even 
sneak these weights between the larger plates if you wish to help a colleague break through some largely 
psychological barrier.
9. Use any of the contrast training methods discussed earlier.
10. Change some aspects of your typical training session, such as the order or duration of various exercises.
11. Use supramaximal adaptation training (SAT) methods, which entail actions like taking a load which is 
significantly heavier than your IRM off a rack and supporting it, executing ‘lock-outs’ at the end of range, or 
performing small end-of-rangc repetitions.
12. Alter or improve your technique in problematic exercises. Sometimes your sticking point is due to imperfect 
technique, so that a skilled coach, together with video analysis of your movements, can help you carry out 
the necessary changes. It is unwise to attempt any changes in technique close to any competitions, unless 
there is something seriously inefficient or unsafe in your existing technique.

26. Use assistance exercises to strengthen areas of weakness in the problem exercise
27. Use ‘forced repetitions* with the aid of a training partner (details given earlier in Ch 7.1)
28. Use variable resistance methods such as free weights combined with elastics or chains.
Concluding Remarks
The above summary by no means exhausts the repertoire of methods and variations of resistance training that is 
used in resistance training, but it serves as a rapid reference for the major methods which are most frequently used 
in the training of high-level athletes. It intentionally docs not address several other methods quoted or ’invented' 
by writers in popular bodybuilding magazines, simply because they differ only in name and a few minor details 
from existing methods and do not constitute any major new contribution to the field of strength training.
In applying any of the methods discussed in this section, it is essential that the detailed information 
conccming their mechanisms and use given in earlier chapters be consulted in conjunction with the above 
summaries. It should never be forgotten that no methods operate in isolation of one another; each method has 
immediate and delayed training effects which have significant effects on other methods that follow hours, days or 
even weeks later (e.g. sec 3.3.1, 3.4, 5.3, 5.4 and all Ch 6).
The next section examines a physical conditioning system which is widely used in physiotherapy, but is 
rarely regarded as a means of training the normal athlete, except occasionally in the specific situation of improving 
flexibility. This system, known by the somewhat daunting name of Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation 
or, PNF for short, however, can offer a highly comprehensive strength training system that encompasses and 
augments many of the methods and techniques of resistance exercise.
7.2 PNF as a Training System
Strength training is often regarded as a discipline confined largely to the gymnasium or sports field. 
Unfortunately, this can obscure the fact that it can and does appear in other situations which have little direct 
connection with sport.
In particular, PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) contains many useful techniques which can 
play an important role in the strength training of athletes. It is one of the aims of this section to show that PNF is 
a comprehensive conditioning system which includes not only many of the principles already covered in this 
book, but also adds insights which complement these principles.
PNF is invariably regarded by conditioning coaches as a special type of sophisticated stretching, alongside 
static, ballistic and passive stretching. PNF is far more than just another stretching technique; it is actually an 
entire system o f therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures for rehabilitating 
patients suffering from various musculoskeletal injuries or disabilities. Stretching constitutes but one o f many 
aspects of the full repertoire of PNF methods, yet even those enlightened coaches who use PNF extol only its 
virtues as a stretching system.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

al, 1971; O'Leary et al, 1997; Palmer & Moore, 1989; Vandervoort, 1983). These phenomena and the processes of 
adaptation associated with them form the foundation for fitness development. They determine the continuing rise 
in fitness, despite periodic interruption in the training process (Matveyev, 1964; Mateev 1964; Zimkin, 1965).
Research into the after-effects of muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature. For 
instance, a statistically significant increase in the speed of an unloaded movement was found directly after the 
same movement was executed with a weight (Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962). Conversely, other research 
could not detect such an effect, despite subjective claims by the athletes that their movements felt quicker after 
using loads (Nofsinger, 1963; Nelson & Lamber, 1965). No increase in the vertical jump could be measured 
shortly after preceding resistive exercises (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965). Shot-put results even deteriorated after 
preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
The after-effect has been examined in more detail in Russian research. It has been noted that preliminary 
isometric tension has a positive effect on the subsequent dynamic work. Despite fatigue following isometric 
tension, the effectiveness of dynamic work increases, usually by up to 20% when compared with work executed 
without preliminary isometric tension. 
With the reverse sequence of work, results deteriorate (Shiedin & 
Kunevich, 1935; Vinogradov & Delov, 1938; Vereshchagin, 1956; Farfel, 1964; Uflyand, 1965).
The after-effect occurs immediately after preliminary isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still 
retains some trace of inhibitory influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared 
with its initial level (Leinik, 1951; Vinogradov, 1966). The data indicates that isometric tension under certain 
conditions can serve as a stimulus for dynamic work and play an important role in developing muscular strength.

Research into the after-effects of muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature. For 
instance, a statistically significant increase in the speed of an unloaded movement was found directly after the 
same movement was executed with a weight (Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962). Conversely, other research 
could not detect such an effect, despite subjective claims by the athletes that their movements felt quicker after 
using loads (Nofsinger, 1963; Nelson & Lamber, 1965). No increase in the vertical jump could be measured 
shortly after preceding resistive exercises (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965). Shot-put results even deteriorated after 
preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
The after-effect has been examined in more detail in Russian research. It has been noted that preliminary 
isometric tension has a positive effect on the subsequent dynamic work. Despite fatigue following isometric 
tension, the effectiveness of dynamic work increases, usually by up to 20% when compared with work executed 
without preliminary isometric tension. 
With the reverse sequence of work, results deteriorate (Shiedin & 
Kunevich, 1935; Vinogradov & Delov, 1938; Vereshchagin, 1956; Farfel, 1964; Uflyand, 1965).
The after-effect occurs immediately after preliminary isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still 
retains some trace of inhibitory influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared 
with its initial level (Leinik, 1951; Vinogradov, 1966). The data indicates that isometric tension under certain 
conditions can serve as a stimulus for dynamic work and play an important role in developing muscular strength.

Later in this text, it will be shown that the effective and safe prescription of resistance training should begin with 
an understanding of force-time and related curves concerning the patterns of force production in sport and 
resistance training. On this basis we can identify several major objectives of strength training, namely:
• To increase maximal or absolute strength
• To increase explosive strength (large force in minimal time)
• To increase the Rate of Force Production
• To enable the muscles to generate large forces for a given period
• To enable the muscles to sustain small forces for a prolonged period
• To increase muscle and connective tissue hypertrophy
The summary of training approaches given by Table 1.1 may be adequate for the average personal trainer or coach 
dealing with the average client or lower level athlete, but it needs to be expanded upon to take into account the 
objectives stated above. In particular, it needs to distinguish between methods concentrating on neural adaptation 
versus the different types of hypertrophy and muscle endurance. This is done at length in later chapters.

23:- contrast methods

The use of any shock method under such circumstances is potentially harmful and definitely detrimental to performance. These methods are generally unsuitable for novices and should only be employed by experienced athletes with a solid background of special strength training." The text notes "shock method" was Verkhoshansky's name for the plyometric method when he first formalised it.
30:**When to apply** — An experienced athlete whose strength or power has stalled for a long period despite progressive loading, after overtraining has been excluded. Inference: in a collegiate setting, the check for "overtraining rather than long-term stagnation" would draw on the readiness data already collected (for Eric, mRSI trends, `docs/method-baseline.md` lines 74-75) before choosing a shock method.
32:**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices, and not when the plateau may be fatigue (the text says a shock method is then "potentially harmful and definitely detrimental"). The list gives no dosing; the methods are described elsewhere (7.1). The text gives no rule for distinguishing stagnation from overtraining.
34:**Example** — Inference: a senior lifter whose squat has not moved for months on steady linear loading, with stable readiness markers, might get a short block of maximal eccentrics or contrast work from this list. The text gives no worked example.
---
30:expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with rest between each (an
31:"interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several repetitions with the same
40:**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
44:all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
58:intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
---
16:**What it is** — "The effectiveness of any circuit may be enhanced by taking cognizance of the Setchinov phenomenon, which encourages restoration by means of diverting activity performed between exercises. For example, this may entail exercise of upper body muscles alternating with exercise of unfatigued muscles of the legs. In applying this principle to circuit training, upper body stations should then alternately exercise upper and lower body muscles, back and front muscles, or agonistic and antagonistic muscles" (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308, checked against the page image). The authors' layouts (Figs 5.25-5.28, verified against the page image, PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308; described in the text on PDF pp. 319-320): aerobic stations (AS) alternating one-for-one with resistance stations (RS) that alternate upper and lower body (Fig 5.25); one aerobic station followed by two resistance stations, "again alternately exercising the upper and lower (or front/back, left/right, etc.) parts of the body" (Fig 5.27); and one aerobic station followed by three resistance stations (Fig 5.28). Circuits aimed "more on muscle endurance or strength, can begin with an aerobics station, then progress through a succession of resistance stations, also preferably sequenced in accordance with the Setchinov principle."
18:**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one in the name: diverting activity between exercises "encourages restoration" of the muscles just worked (PDF p. 319 / printed p. 308). They do not explain how. Inference: the Setchinov (Sechenov) active-rest effect is a classical observation that working other muscles during a rest period speeds recovery of the fatigued ones; the book cites no study for it here, and its size in modern studies is not checked in this entry.

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 7 lead-in and 7.1 (10 entries), Opus independent reviewer

Date: 2026-10-03. Scope: the 10 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch7a.txt`. Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, PDF idx 404-414 (printed 393-403), plus PDF 175 (printed 164), PDF 21-22 (printed 10-11), PDF 315 (printed 304) and PDF 335-336 (printed 324-325) for cross-references. PDF idx = printed + 11.

How checked: full text layer of PDF 404-414, 175, 21, 22, 315, 335-336. Page images opened for PDF 405, 406 (300 dpi, plus three full-resolution crops of Fig 7.2), 408, 409, 410, 411, 412, 413, 414 and 175 (renders in `staging/_renders/r7a_p*.png`). Every number quoted in the entries was matched against the page image as well as the text layer, because the text layer garbles some of them ("3*6 sets", "1*3 repetitions", "I RM", "I Classical" for "A. Classical"). All 13 "Eric's baseline" quotes were checked against `docs/method-baseline.md` lines 30, 41, 61, 76, 103, 104, 107, 109, 119, 142, 180, 182 and 186. Quotes, line numbers and provenance tags all match. Every `[[wikilink]]` in the 10 files resolves to a file in the vault or the staging library.

## Confidence rule applied to all 10

The brief sets `supported` as the ceiling for training prescriptions and `untested` for anecdotes. The folder applies this unevenly. Table 1.1 (`framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal`, "based largely on the practical experience of generations of bodybuilders and weightlifters") and DeLorme/Oxford are `supported`. The Ch5 circuit-layout catalogue is `untested`. This review uses one rule:

- **`supported`**: a prescription with parameters that the book presents as established practice in the strength sports, such as "one of the best known", "commonly used" or "popularly used". This matches the Table 1.1 entry.
- **`untested`**: a single anecdote; a bodybuilding novelty the authors themselves discount; a list of tips given without basis; or a taxonomy whose only empirical claim is an unevidenced ordering.
- **`contested`**: only where the entry shows a same-question conflict, and with the reason scoped to the claim actually in conflict.

| Entry | Current | Deserves | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Figs 7.1 and 7.2 chart | untested | untested (keep) | A taxonomy. Its one empirical claim is the "increasing importance of nervous system training" arrow, which has no evidence (PDF 405). The deficit rule is rated `contested` in its own linked entry. |
| Maximal / supramaximal / circa-max / submax | contested | contested (keep, scope it) | The definitions themselves would be `supported`. Keeping `contested` follows the Ch1 lesson, provided the reason is scoped to the one rest figure (see FIX). |
| Three bodybuilding regimes | untested | **supported** | Parameterised prescriptions the book calls "one of the best known elementary bodybuilding methods", with add-ons "popularly used" (PDF 408). Same footing as Table 1.1. |
| Set structures | untested | **supported** | Parameterised prescriptions. Plateau is "commonly used" (PDF 408), pyramids carry %1RM values "derived from the equations associated with Fig 1.9" (PDF 409), and DeLorme/APRE (rated `supported` and `contested` elsewhere) are named as pyramid forms. |
| Interval training and cluster sets | contested | contested (keep) | A real same-paragraph conflict on cluster load, and stronger than the entry shows (see FIX). |
| Hybrid repetitions and sets | untested | untested (keep) | The examples are the authors' own constructions ("may be devised by the inventive coach", PDF 411). No practice base or data is given beyond the clean-and-jerk. |
| Progressive and random segmental | untested | untested (keep) | One anecdote (Rigert) with no outcome reported. |
| Contrast methods | contested | contested (keep, scope it to heavy-light) | See FIX. |
| Miscellaneous bodybuilding sets | untested | untested (keep) | The authors frame these as novelties "of minimal significance" for sport (PDF 412). |
| 27 sticking-point strategies | untested | untested (keep) | A list of tips ("Among some of the methods are the following", PDF 413) with no basis given for most items. |

## Voice

No first-person Siff passage and no third-person "Verkhoshansky" passage appears anywhere on PDF 404-414. The "you" in the sticking-point list (PDF 413-414) and in Peak Contraction Sets (PDF 413) is instructional second person, not authorial first person. All 10 entries therefore correctly write "the authors", as the brief requires when a passage cannot be assigned to one author. No entry presents Eric's or the writer's view as the authors'. The attribution problems listed below are unlabelled writer inferences.

## Entry verdicts

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| framework--strength-training-aims-and-method-chart-figs-7-1-and-7-2.md | **GO** | None found. | checked: Fig 7.1 boxes, caption and arrow direction against the PDF 405 image. Fig 7.2 at 300 dpi plus crops (PDF 406): all four column headers; 8 quality boxes, with connectors only from Explosive Strength (to Reactive), Flexibility (to the static/passive/active/ballistic/PNF box) and Hypertrophy (to Bodybuilding Methods), so "five of eight have no drawn link" is correct; Reactive connects to both Plyometrics and Contrast; Supramaximal runs straight to its variations box; Maximal, Circa-maximal and Submaximal have no connector; Quasi-isometrics and Endurance Methods have no variations; Oxford Method floats unlinked; Weightlifting, Isometrics, Pyramiding, Bodybuilding, Circuit and Multi-purpose each connect to their variation boxes; Stripping appears twice and APRE twice; every variation list matches. Quotes at PDF 404-405 / printed 393-394 and the concluding remark at PDF 414 / printed 403. Chapter 1 deficit quotes at PDF 21 / printed 10, including "5RM to 8RM". Baseline lines 76 and 103 quoted and tagged correctly. Rating `untested` is consistent with the rule above. |
| framework--maximal-supramaximal-circa-maximal-and-submaximal-methods.md | **FIX** | (1) The "Why `contested`" paragraph says "Both sentences describe the rest between near-maximal singles in weightlifting training". PDF 406 frames its 1-5 min as "This 1RM set with optimal recovery intervals **between sets**". The PDF 409 sentence ("single repetitions of near-maximal weights with a few seconds of rest between repetitions") opens the interval-training section and leads straight into Cluster Training ("10-20 second interval between each repetition ... in an extended set", PDF 409). So the two passages may describe different methods (sets of singles against clustered singles in one extended set). The conflict is real as worded, but it is not certain they answer the same question. (2) The entry carries `contested` because of one rest figure, but the entry is four categories of definitions, so a reader filtering by confidence would read the load bands as disputed. (3) "When NOT to apply" says "the authors class eccentrics, forced reps and cheating as higher-risk methods (PDF p. 407)". PDF 407 gives an injury warning for eccentrics ("carries an increased risk of injury") and for cheating ("if injury is to be avoided"), but none for forced repetitions. | (1) After the first sentence of "Why `contested`", add: "PDF 406 calls the 1-5 minutes 'optimal recovery intervals between sets', and the PDF 409 sentence opens the interval section that leads straight into cluster training (10-20 s within an extended set), so the two passages may describe different methods, sets of singles against clustered singles. The book does not say which." Change "Both sentences describe" to "As worded, both sentences describe". (2) Start that paragraph with: "The rating applies only to the rest between near-maximal singles; the load-band definitions are not in dispute." (3) Change to "the authors give injury warnings for eccentrics and cheating (PDF p. 407); forced repetitions sit in the same supramaximal group" or delete "forced reps". |
| framework--three-bodybuilding-regimes-and-add-on-methods.md | **FIX** | (1) Confidence `untested` understates. These are parameterised prescriptions the book calls "one of the best known elementary bodybuilding methods" and "popularly used" (PDF 408 / printed 397), the same basis as the `supported` Table 1.1 entry. (2) "When to apply": "Split routines and zone training suit athletes who lift on more days than a whole-body session allows." The authors say only that zone training "must be spread over several sessions or days" (PDF 409). The sentence sits after an "Inference:" sentence, so its label scope is unclear. Everything else checks: the table values (3-5 x 8-10, 2-5 min; 15-20 at 60-70%, 2-3 min; 5-8 at 80-90%, 2-5 min), the "A." label (image), Table 1.1's 60-80 / 8-15 / 4-8 / 2-5 (PDF 22 / printed 11), the supersets, pre-exhaustion and split-week quotes, and baseline lines 61, 104 and 180. | (1) Set `confidence: supported`. (2) Prefix: "Inference: split routines and zone training suit athletes who lift on more days than a whole-body session allows." |
| framework--set-structures-plateau-step-stripping-and-pyramids.md | **FIX** | (1) Confidence `untested` understates, as above. Plateau is "commonly used" (PDF 408) and the pyramid values are "derived from the equations associated with Fig 1.9" (PDF 409). (2) Unlabelled writer claims: "Step sets to find a working load for a fixed repetition target" ("When to apply"), and "Plateau sets are for novices and transition phases, not for a peaking block" ("When NOT to apply"). The authors give the plateau's use (PDF 408) but say nothing about peaking, and give no purpose for the step method. All numbers check against the PDF 408-409 images: 50x10/70x6 x3, 60-85 x3, the 5-10 kg strip, "no more than 6 repetitions", both pyramids, 2-6 min, 4 to 10, 2.5-5 kg, the "rarely used by serious athletes" quote and item 7 (PDF 413). | (1) Set `confidence: supported`. (2) Rewrite as "Inference: step sets can find a working load for a fixed repetition target" and "Plateau sets are for novices and transition phases (PDF p. 408). Inference: not for a peaking block." |
| framework--interval-resistance-training-and-cluster-sets.md | **FIX** | The contested reason is correct but incomplete, and it leans on the weaker evidence. The same paragraph that sets "Characteristically, the minimum load used is one's 5RM" (PDF 409 / printed 398, image) also prescribes extensive clustering "with one's **4-6RM**" (a 6RM is lighter than a 5RM) and a stripping variant where "the load is decreased by 10-20%" after each set (PDF 409-410). Both fall below the stated minimum in the text itself, without any %1RM conversion. The entry's 75-90% argument depends on reading the pyramid's "6 x 85%" as a 6RM, an inference (correctly labelled). All other values check against the PDF 409-410 images: 30-40% / 5-6 x 20-30 / 1-2 min; 50-60% / 3-6 sets to failure / 10-90 s; ">180 beats/min"; circuits 1-3 min; "75% of (220-Age)". The Ch5 comparison (20-40 reps at ≤30% against 3-8 reps at >70%) checks at PDF 315 / printed 304. Baseline lines 119 and 182 are correct. | In "Why `contested`", lead with the direct text: "The same paragraph sets the minimum at 'one's 5RM' (PDF p. 409) but prescribes extensive clustering 'with one's 4-6RM' and a stripping form that cuts the load 'by 10-20%' each set (PDF pp. 409-410), both below that minimum; intensive clustering then gives '75-90% of 1RM' (PDF p. 410)." Keep the existing pyramid-based Inference after it as supporting reasoning. |
| framework--hybrid-repetitions-and-hybrid-sets.md | **FIX** (minor) | (1) "When to apply — When session time or space is short and several movements can be loaded by the same bar". The authors say only "Instead of doing three separate exercises at three different stations, one can do all of them in a single repetition or at a single station" (PDF 410). Time and space are the writer's addition and are unlabelled. (2) The superscript is left "Unclear as printed ... Inference: the superscript may be a set count". The book settles this itself: the 6.6.2 convention writes 80 kg x 6 done twice as "6(80)²", with the superscript as the set count, and gives the hybrid example "100 / 2+3+1" (PDF 336 / printed 325). The PDF 411 image shows 80³ over 3+5+2, so the notation means 3 sets, and the book's "for a set of 3 repetitions" is a slip in its own wording. All other content checks against the PDF 410-411 images, including both example lists and the two guidelines. | (1) Prefix "Inference:" to the time/space clause, or replace it with "When a circuit is to be condensed into one station (PDF p. 410)." (2) Replace the unclear note with: "By the 6.6.2 convention (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, where '6(80)²' means two sets of 6 at 80 kg) the superscript is the number of sets, so 80³ over 3+5+2 means three sets of the 10-repetition hybrid; the text's 'for a set of 3 repetitions' conflicts with its own convention." |
| heuristic--progressive-and-random-segmental-training.md | **FIX** (minor) | "When to apply": "The random variant when a long block of one exercise has stalled." The authors give the random variant a preventive purpose, "to minimise the possibility of early accommodation to a predictable regime" (PDF 410 / printed 399, image), not a remedy for a stall. The sentence sits outside the preceding "Inference:" sentence. All quotes check against the PDF 410 image, including "2-4 segments", "3-7 repetitions", Twenty-Ones, Rigert's three segments of 1-3 reps, and "Frequently ... full clean pull". | Replace with: "The random variant from the start of a block, to limit early accommodation (the authors' stated purpose, PDF p. 410)." If the stall use is wanted, write it as "Inference: ...". |
| framework--contrast-methods-load-release-pneumatics-heavy-light-set.md | **FIX** | (1) Scope. The entry says "The heavy-light set and load release rest on exactly the effect those studies dispute." The 3.4.2 Western studies test "the speed of an unloaded movement ... directly after the same movement was executed with a weight" (PDF 175 / printed 164, image). That is a preceding loaded effort followed by a lighter one, which is the heavy-light set. Load release and pneumatics drop the load inside one repetition. The authors give a different mechanism for them ("the contrast in stimulus ... produces a rapid acceleration", PDF 411), and the cited studies did not test it. (2) The evidence is reported one-sided. The same page, PDF 175, reports the Russian side: "Dynamic work with heavy weights (i.e. high tension with relatively few repetitions) also elicits a positive after-effect in the central nervous system ... and an improvement in speed and strength" (Portnov 1955 and others), and "intense preliminary strength tension improves results in jumping exercises ... in shotputting ... and in rowing". "When NOT to apply" says only "the book's own cited Western studies found none in several tasks". That is the one-sided reading the Ch1 lesson forbids. All method definitions and the 20% / 10-20 s / 3-5 rep figures check against the PDF 411 image, and the Ch5 shock-method link (contrast methods listed, "unsuitable for novices") checks. | (1) In "Why `contested`", change "The heavy-light set and load release rest on" to "The heavy-light set rests on". Add: "Load release and pneumatics unload within a single repetition; the cited studies did not test that, so the conflict does not reach them directly." - **`untested`**: a single anecdote; a bodybuilding novelty the authors themselves discount; a list of tips given without basis; or a taxonomy whose only empirical claim is an unevidenced ordering.
- **`contested`**: only where the entry shows a same-question conflict, and with the reason scoped to the claim actually in conflict.

| Three bodybuilding regimes | untested | **supported** | Parameterised prescriptions the book calls "one of the best known elementary bodybuilding methods", with add-ons "popularly used" (PDF 408). Same footing as Table 1.1. |
| Set structures | untested | **supported** | Parameterised prescriptions. Plateau is "commonly used" (PDF 408), pyramids carry %1RM values "derived from the equations associated with Fig 1.9" (PDF 409), and DeLorme/APRE (rated `supported` and `contested` elsewhere) are named as pyramid forms. |

| Hybrid repetitions and sets | untested | untested (keep) | The examples are the authors' own constructions ("may be devised by the inventive coach", PDF 411). No practice base or data is given beyond the clean-and-jerk. |
| Progressive and random segmental | untested | untested (keep) | One anecdote (Rigert) with no outcome reported. |
